title: Find the largest / smallest element in an array (single pass, O(n)).
shortTitle: Find the Largest and Smallest Element in an Array
keyPoints: Seed both max and min with the first element, then scan once, updating each when you see something bigger or smaller.
A single pass gives both answers in O(n) time and O(1) space, which is strictly better than sorting at O(n log n).
Seed with the first real element, not zero, because amounts can be negative debits.
For money use BigDecimal and compareTo for correct value comparison.
The pairwise optimisation reduces comparisons from 2n to 1.5n by processing elements in pairs.
Return both results together in one pass rather than scanning the array twice.

s1_definition.oneliner: Seed max and min with the first element, then scan once, updating each when you see something bigger or smaller.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Single pass** – iterate once from left to right, tracking both the maximum and minimum simultaneously.
- **Two trackers** – initialise both `max` and `min` with the first element of the array.
- **O(n) time** – each element is visited once, with two comparisons per element.
- **O(1) space** – only two tracking variables are needed.
- **Better than sorting** – sorting costs O(n log n) and is overkill when only two values are needed.
s1_definition.analogy: The fraud desk at National Bank of India wants both the biggest and the smallest transaction on Rajesh's account today. Instead of sorting the whole day's list, a clerk simply walks down the list once, remembering the biggest seen so far and the smallest seen so far, updating both as new amounts appear. By the end of one pass, the clerk has both answers.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the largest and smallest elements of an array is a single linear pass. I seed both a maximum and a minimum tracker with the first element, then walk the rest of the array once, updating the maximum when I see a larger value and the minimum when I see a smaller value. One pass gives both answers in linear time with constant extra space, which beats sorting.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this on the fraud desk, where the biggest transaction of the day is a red flag for an unusually large transfer and the smallest can be a tiny test transaction that often precedes fraud. Scanning the day's amounts once gives both, exactly, in BigDecimal.

I mention the pairwise optimisation that cuts comparisons by about a quarter by comparing elements in pairs first, though I note the simple version is clearer. I always return both results together so the caller gets them from a single scan.

Remember one sentence: seed both trackers with the first element, scan once, and update each when you find something bigger or smaller.
